theme_definition: Economic exposure to rising strategic demand, policy support, and supply-chain reorientation intended to expand secure Western access to critical minerals.
directional_shock: An increase in strategic demand and policy support for secure Western critical-mineral supply chains, together with pressure to reduce dependence on concentrated or geopolitically vulnerable supply.
cutoff_rule: Use only supplied SEC text filed on or before the applicable quarterly cutoff. Do not use pretrained knowledge, company-name inference, embeddings, prices, or returns.

mechanisms.definition: Exploration, development, mining, or production of critical-mineral ores or feedstocks.
mechanisms.positive_logic: Higher demand, prices, financing, or policy support may benefit viable producers and developers.
mechanisms.negative_logic: Permitting, geopolitical, cost, grade, financing, or project-execution exposure may impair the firm.

mechanisms.definition: Separation, refining, smelting, purification, precursor production, or other processing of critical-mineral inputs.
mechanisms.positive_logic: Domestic or allied processing capacity may gain from localization incentives and constrained capacity.
mechanisms.negative_logic: Input scarcity, energy costs, technology constraints, or concentrated foreign processing may harm operations.

mechanisms.definition: Recovery, recycling, reuse, or circular processing of critical minerals from batteries, electronics, scrap, or waste.
mechanisms.positive_logic: Scarcity and localization policy may increase demand for recovered material.
mechanisms.negative_logic: Weak collection economics, volatile commodity prices, or process limitations may impair returns.

mechanisms.definition: Equipment, engineering, chemicals, logistics, power, water, or infrastructure materially enabling mineral extraction or processing.
mechanisms.positive_logic: Capacity expansion may increase demand for enabling goods and services.
mechanisms.negative_logic: Project delays or mineral-sector contraction may reduce demand.

mechanisms.definition: Battery cells, components, cathodes, anodes, energy storage, or battery manufacturing materially dependent on critical minerals.
mechanisms.positive_logic: Strategic demand and subsidies may expand production or improve access to support.
mechanisms.negative_logic: Mineral scarcity or price increases may raise costs and constrain output.

mechanisms.definition: Vehicles, charging, motors, power electronics, or electrified transport with material critical-mineral dependence.
mechanisms.positive_logic: Policy-supported electrification may raise demand for products.
mechanisms.negative_logic: Input costs, sourcing rules, or shortages may compress margins or delay production.

mechanisms.definition: Electronics, semiconductors, magnets, optical products, or communications equipment materially dependent on critical-mineral inputs.
mechanisms.positive_logic: Secure specialized supply or substitution capability may confer an advantage.
mechanisms.negative_logic: Concentrated supply, export restrictions, or shortages may disrupt production.

mechanisms.definition: Renewable generation, transmission, nuclear, turbines, or grid systems with material critical-mineral requirements.
mechanisms.positive_logic: Infrastructure investment may increase product demand.
mechanisms.negative_logic: Commodity costs or sourcing restrictions may impair project economics.

mechanisms.definition: Technology that substitutes away from constrained minerals or materially reduces mineral intensity.
mechanisms.positive_logic: Scarcity and policy pressure may increase adoption of substitution or efficiency technologies.
mechanisms.negative_logic: A substitution threat may reduce demand for an incumbent mineral-linked product.

mechanisms.definition: Material dependence on mineral supply, processing, customers, or facilities in a concentrated or strategically sensitive geography.
mechanisms.positive_logic: Diversified allied sourcing may offer resilience or policy eligibility.
mechanisms.negative_logic: Concentration, trade restrictions, sanctions, or export controls may disrupt supply or demand.

mechanisms.definition: Material grants, tax credits, loans, procurement, offtake, or regulation specifically tied to secure critical-mineral supply chains.
mechanisms.positive_logic: Direct support or procurement may improve demand, financing, or project economics.
mechanisms.negative_logic: Eligibility restrictions, policy withdrawal, or compliance costs may impair economics.

mechanisms.definition: Material exposure to the price or availability of critical-mineral inputs without a stronger operational mechanism above.
mechanisms.positive_logic: Ownership of inventory, pricing power, or pass-through clauses may provide upside.
mechanisms.negative_logic: Higher input prices or shortages may compress margins or constrain production.

interpretive_note: Mineral mention alone is insufficient. The supplied passage must support a material business relationship, dependency, project, policy linkage, operational constraint, or enabling role. Copper and other broad commodities require especially specific evidence because not every use is thematic.
